title: Alternative DAG Parameterizations
text:
Overview
This living research book develops and evaluates alternative parameterizations of directed acyclic graphs. Its scientific scope will be refined as source materials and research questions are introduced.

title: Alternative DAG Parameterizations
text:
Abstract
The project is at the setup stage. No project-specific theoretical or empirical conclusions have been established. The executable Monte Carlo example in the appendix demonstrates the computational workflow only.

title: Alternative DAG Parameterizations
text:
Reading guide
The main text follows a scientific article structure: introduction, related work, notation, methods, research results, discussion, conclusions, and references. Topic investigations can expand the results section over time. Appendices document reproducibility and the evolution of the research.
Each substantive claim should be linked to a derivation, verified source, or reproducible computation, with its assumptions and limitations stated explicitly.

title: Appendix A — Reproducible computation: workflow demonstration
text:
A.1 Question and status
Status: demonstration. Can a standalone R script supply the book’s table and figure without copying results by hand?

title: Appendix A — Reproducible computation: workflow demonstration
text:
A.2 Mathematical expectation
For independent standard normal observations, the sample mean has expectation zero and standard deviation \(1/\sqrt{n}\). This is a theoretical result; the simulation illustrates its numerical behavior.

title: Appendix A — Reproducible computation: workflow demonstration
text:
A.3 Method and script
The downloadable R script uses seed 20261010, 2,000 repetitions, and sample sizes 10, 100, and 1,000. Run it independently from the repository root:
Rscript scripts/R/001-monte-carlo.R
The book executes that same script when rendered:

title: Appendix A — Reproducible computation: workflow demonstration
text:
A.4 Interpretation and limitations
Table A.1 and Figure A.1 compare simulated variability with the analytical prediction. Differences reflect finite Monte Carlo sampling. A simulation can provide evidence or a counterexample; it does not replace a general mathematical proof.
This example does not establish any I-MAP finding.
